name: DoS attack construction and countermeasure/responsibility analysis
theory_paragraphs: A \term{denial-of-service (DoS) attack} targets \term{availability} in the CIA triad: it prevents or impairs the authorized use of networks, systems or applications by \imp{exhausting or damaging a resource}. The exhausted resource can be \emph{bandwidth} (flood the bottleneck link, e.g. ICMP/UDP floods), \emph{state} (fill a connection, subscription or memory table, e.g. SYN flood, mass forged registrations), \emph{computation} (force expensive work per cheap request, e.g. signature verification, recursive decompression, zip bombs), or \emph{software correctness} (crash via buffer overflow, unhandled exception, resource leak). A \term{distributed DoS (DDoS)} multiplies the volume with a \term{botnet} of compromised zombies (e.g. Mirai, 2016: $\approx 500{,}000$ IoT devices, $\approx 665$~Gbps against Krebs on Security and up to $\approx 1.2$~Tbps against the Dyn DNS servers).

\begin{tightitem}\item \term{Source address spoofing}: UDP and ICMP are \term{connectionless}, so the claimed source IP is never verified --- Mallory writes the victim's address as the source. TCP's three-way handshake proves the source (it must receive the SYN-ACK), so TCP source addresses cannot be blindly spoofed.\item \term{Reflection}: Mallory sends small requests carrying the victim's spoofed source to many servers; \emph{the servers} reply to the victim, hiding the attacker and adding their bandwidth to the flood.\item \term{Amplification}: a small request triggers a much larger reply (a 60-byte DNS query can yield a 4 KB response, $\approx 60\times$). \imp{Attacker bandwidth does not matter --- the reflector supplies it.}\end{tightitem}

\term{SYN flood}: on receiving a SYN the server stores a \emph{pending} entry in its \term{connection table} and waits for the final ACK. Flooding SYNs with spoofed (non-responding) sources fills the table with half-open entries, so \imp{legitimate connections can no longer be accepted}. This works even when the attacker has less bandwidth than the victim, because each cheap SYN costs the server a table slot until timeout. Defenses: (i) time out pending connections aggressively, (ii) limit half-open connections per source IP, (iii) \term{SYN cookies}: encode the table row (encrypted and MACed) inside the TCP header/sequence number so \emph{no state is committed} until the client returns it with the ACK.

Countermeasure logic: fix spoofing \emph{at the source} with \term{ingress/egress filtering} (BCP 38): the attacker's ISP drops packets whose source address is inconsistent with its routing tables, at the network edge. \imp{Victim-side dropping cannot work --- the upstream link is already congested before the packets arrive.} At the service side: authenticate the \emph{whole} message (MAC/signature, with a nonce or timestamp against replay), verify the source before committing memory or computation, prefer TCP or a challenge-response handshake, rate-limit requests, and add redundancy across providers. \term{Responsibility}: the ISP deploys filtering; the service fixes its own authentication and resource-commitment logic; the victim and its cloud provider cannot help once the upstream link is saturated.
theory_cheatsheet: DoS = attack on \term{availability}: exhaust bandwidth, state, computation, or correctness.
UDP/ICMP source IPs are forgeable (connectionless); the TCP handshake verifies the source.
\term{Reflection} $+$ \term{amplification}: spoof the victim's IP and let big servers flood it (DNS: 60 B $\rightarrow$ 4 KB).
\term{SYN flood} fills the half-open connection table; fix with SYN cookies, timeouts, per-IP caps.
Amplification factor $=$ bytes or work triggered $\, / \,$ bytes or work the attacker sends.
\imp{Ingress filtering (BCP 38) belongs to the attacker's ISP} --- victim-side filtering fails because the upstream link is already full.
identify_givens: A request--response or publish--subscribe service/protocol described message by message, usually over UDP with spoofable source IP addresses and weak or missing source authentication (no MAC/signature over the whole message, or a check covering only part of the message). An attacker model is stated: the attacker has less bandwidth than the victim, may eavesdrop or intercept traffic, but cannot recover keys. Sometimes a named flood (SYN/ICMP) or a service whose work-per-request is expensive or whose replies are much larger than the requests.
identify_target: Describe concretely how the attacker performs a DoS against a stated victim (the server itself or a third-party client) despite having less bandwidth; then describe how the vulnerability can be countered and, when asked, who must deploy the countermeasure (the attacker's ISP, the service, or the cloud provider).
identify_keywords: describe how this vulnerability can be countered
strategy_name: Exploit spoofing + asymmetry (amplification or state exhaustion), then authenticate the source

algorithm.detail: List each protocol message with its transport and effect:\begin{tightitem}\item transport: UDP/ICMP $\rightarrow$ \term{source IP is forgeable}; TCP $\rightarrow$ handshake-verified source;\item effect: what work or traffic each message triggers at the server (replies, stored state per client, downstream messages to third parties).\end{tightitem}

Check what actually authenticates the sender. An unauthenticated UDP source field can simply be forged. A subtler gap: only \emph{part} of the message is protected (e.g. only $X = E(IP_i, K_i)$ is verified while $L$ travels in plaintext), so a man in the middle tampers with the unprotected fields.

Spot the \term{amplification factor} (one small request triggers many or large replies: $L$ bytes split into 512~KB blocks, or one publish causes one message per subscriber per topic) or the \term{exhaustion target} (server CPU per verification, memory, connection table or thread pool grows per forged request or half-open SYN).

Combine the gap and the asymmetry:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{reflection/amplification}: spoof the victim's IP (or raise the unprotected $L$) so the server floods the victim with traffic;\item \term{state/computation exhaustion}: mass-forge requests so the server's own memory, table or CPU saturates.\end{tightitem}State explicitly why \emph{less bandwidth than the victim} does not matter: \imp{the server supplies the bandwidth and the state}.

Authenticate the \emph{whole} message and verify the source before committing resources: use TCP (the handshake proves the source address) or sign/MAC/encrypt everything, e.g. $E(IP_i \,\|\, L, K_i)$ so tampering with $L$ is detected; add a nonce/sequence number/expiration against \term{replay}; commit no memory or computation until the source is proven (challenge-response); add rate limiting.

If asked who deploys what: \begin{tightitem}\item spoofing is fixed at the source by the \term{attacker's ISP} via ingress/egress filtering (BCP 38);\item victim-side or cloud-provider filtering fails because \imp{the upstream link is already congested};\item the service fixes its own authentication, resource-commitment logic and (for SYN floods) SYN cookies/backlog handling.\end{tightitem}

variations.name: Tampering instead of spoofing
variations.detail: In dasak19 P1 the protocol does authenticate the client ($D(X, K_i) = IP_i$ is checked), so pure IP spoofing fails --- the trap is to overlook that $L$ is sent in \emph{plaintext}: a man in the middle raises $L$ and gets amplification anyway. Adapt Step 2: enumerate which fields lie \emph{inside} the authenticated portion and attack the ones outside.

variations.name: Victim is the server, not a client
variations.detail: In dasak18 P1 the attacker targets the server itself: mass forged subscriptions exhaust server memory, or one forged publish forces the server to emit hundreds of messages. Adapt Step 4: choose between \term{traffic amplification} against third parties and \term{state/resource exhaustion} of the server --- the official solution accepts either.

variations.name: Role reversal: replay to force expensive work
variations.detail: Some sittings replace spoofing with \term{replay}: unauthenticated (or nonce-less signed) messages are re-sent to force repeated expensive server work (malware scans, many hash comparisons). The fix still follows Step 5: nonce/timestamp inside the signed portion plus rate limiting.

variations.name: Named flood with responsibility question
variations.detail: 2022/NEN-style variants name the threat (SYN flood, ICMP flood, amplification via open resolvers) and ask \emph{who must act}. Trap: saying the victim or its cloud provider should filter --- the upstream link is already saturated, so ingress filtering (BCP 38) belongs to the attacker's ISP; SYN floods additionally need cookies/backlog fixes at the server.

original_problem: Denial of service. To save battery, a fleet of constrained parking sensors offloads cryptographic work to a verification oracle O run by the city. The protocol is as follows (all messages sent over UDP): To request a check, sensor $S_i$ sends $\langle IP_i, IP_O, C, M, \sigma \rangle$ to O, where $C$ is the claimed signer's certificate, $M$ a firmware manifest, and $\sigma$ the signature to verify. O performs a full certificate-chain validation and signature verification (about 40~ms of CPU per request), then sends a \emph{verification report} back to $IP_i$: a 4~KB document containing the parsed certificate chain, every intermediate CRL entry consulted, and the verdict. Describe how a malicious user can abuse this service to mount a denial-of-service attack, given that the attacker has less bandwidth than the victim, and describe how the vulnerability can be countered.

original_steps.work: Flows: a single \emph{verify-request} (sensor $\rightarrow$ O) triggers (a) expensive CPU work at O --- chain validation plus signature verification, $\approx 40$~ms per request --- and (b) a 4~KB report sent to the claimed source address. Everything is UDP, so the source IP of every request can be forged.

Authentication gap: the request carries no credential, MAC or proof of source --- O trusts the claimed $IP_i$ field of a spoofable UDP datagram and starts computing (and replying) before any source verification has taken place.

Asymmetry (two kinds): (a) \emph{traffic amplification}: one $\approx 200$-byte request makes O emit a 4~KB report ($\approx 20\times$) to an address of the attacker's choosing; (b) \emph{computational exhaustion}: each cheap request burns $\approx 40$~ms of O's CPU, so a modest request rate from the attacker saturates all of O's worker cores.

Attack on a victim host: Mallory sends a stream of verify-requests with the \emph{victim's} IP as source; O reflects a 4~KB report per request and floods the victim's link --- Mallory's small uplink suffices because O supplies the bandwidth. Simultaneously, attack on O itself: the forged requests keep O's CPUs at 100\% on chain validation, so \emph{legitimate sensors} wait indefinitely --- a denial of service with far less bandwidth than O's own link capacity.

Countermeasures at the service: commit no work before the source is proven --- switch to TCP (the handshake verifies the source address) or use a \term{challenge-response cookie}: O first replies with a cheap nonce and only starts validation when the requester returns it, which a spoofer cannot do. Authenticate the \emph{whole} request with a MAC/signature over $\langle IP_i, C, M, \sigma, \text{nonce} \rangle$; rate-limit reports per destination IP and cap CPU per request.

Responsibility: spoofing is eliminated at the source by the \emph{attacker's ISP} deploying ingress/egress filtering (BCP 38), dropping packets whose source address does not match its routing tables. Dropping the reflected reports at the victim (or its cloud provider) does not help, because the victim's upstream link is already congested by the time the packets arrive. O itself must fix the commit-work-before-verification design.
